title: The Austin band's drive against Ashcraft's school bands
summary: Ashcraft recounts a battle of bands where the Austin band outplayed his and argues the growing beat owed little to New Orleans until the Rhythm Kings.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel

blocks.x: No, they did not. And I've often wondered where the influence crept in without their knowing it, and I suspect, of course, it was through Paul Merez and Rapolo, and those fellows. And Brunus. One thing that used to surprise me, I originally played with a little band around a country day school. This must have been as early as 20. Five, four pieces. Not a Dixie-Line combination at all, but with a C-molly saxophone, that kind of lead. When I graduated, I think by learning how to play an E-flat, to the New Trier group, which is a little more sophisticated, they were more sure of themselves, and they were inclined to wad up it a little more. And they were playing pop tunes. This was the day of, let's say, Avalon, well, San, from World War I, Japanese San Man type. But you could still play them in tempo, all right. Pretty good tempo. Then the San Band, maybe just because it was a tougher... San High School. Yeah. The San Band was inclined to really plaster these tunes. I mean, they really hit them. So there was a decided beat to what they were doing. When we ran into the Austin Band, of course, they blew us right out of the room. I can remember when we had a battle of music that was very common those days in the Sovereign Hotel on the north side for, I think it was a San Prom or something like that, where we were at opposite ends of the auditorium. They'd take a vote at the end of a battle, and we won it, hands down, because they could dance to us, and they couldn't dance to the others, or at least they didn't know how. It was a very amicable proceeding, since the Austin boys knew that we'd given our shirts if we'd been able to play as well as they did.
Do you remember anybody in the San Band of that period?

I think Bill Tell, a banjo player, who later played with those Vocalion Wolverines records, was one. I'd have a lot of trouble putting it. Oh, Roz Metzger. We had two pianos. Roz Metzger, who went on and became quite a darn good piano. He's now president of Footcone and Bellingham. It was led by a violinist, like the Ramblers. The reason I brought that up was because I think this increasing attention to beat, as the bands that I ran through got to be a little better, to the point of the Austin band growing the same way, but with more confidence and more intention to really wallop this music and get a thing going, was pretty much independent of New Orleans. At least it was until you heard the Rhythm Kings, because the Rhythm Kings records, they rarely could, I don't think even then they could record with a bass drum.

Don't impress you as being a walloping type of thing. And when you heard the Rhythm Kings, the thing that impressed you more than anything else was the rhythm that they had going without a high volume.
